SEC11A-01.note: 'the geologists ... concluded' is a main clause, so the participial phrase must open a new sentence; C is a comma splice, B dangles the participle onto the first clause, D is fused. PHASE 2: Key and reasoning sound.

SEC11A-02.note: Long subject with two which-clauses; comma closes the nonrestrictive clause before main verb 'shows'. A folds 'shows' into the relative clause leaving no main verb (strong trap); D mismatches the opening comma; C fragment. PHASE 2: Key and reasoning sound; good item.

SEC11A-03.note: 'That the two ... descend' is a noun-clause subject of 'was not demonstrated', so a boundary is needed before it. A misreads as a relative clause on 'vocabulary'; B comma splice; D 'so that' changes sense and leaves 'was' subjectless. PHASE 2: Key and reasoning sound; noun-clause subject is a genuine hard-route skill.

SEC11A-04.note: Standard boundary; 'its oak hull ... had begun' is a full clause. A splice, B fused, C 'with its ... had begun' ungrammatical. Same option template as A-06. PHASE 2: Sound, but shares an identical option template (', its' / none / ', with its' / boundary) with A-06; ship only one of the two in a form.

SEC11A-05.note: 'only after ... did the astronomers recognize' is an inverted independent clause; needs comma + FANBOYS. A splice, B fused, D 'even after' cannot trigger inversion and changes sense. PHASE 2: Sound; inversion is the discriminating feature.

SEC11A-06.note: Second clause has subject 'charred barley and ... loom weights' with verb 'suggest'; semicolon. C 'alongside' strips the subject from 'suggest'. Same comma / none / comma+preposition / boundary template as A-04. PHASE 2: Sound; same template as A-04 (comma / none / comma+preposition / semicolon) - template repetition is a cross-item tell if both appear together.

SEC11B-01.note: Heavy-NP shift: 'singled out [as ...] the steady withdrawal' - the NP is the postposed direct object, so no punctuation. C colon tempting but the preceding clause is incomplete (transitive verb lacking object); B separates verb from object; D adds a stray verb. PHASE 2: Sound; strongest item in the batch (heavy-NP shift, colon trap).

SEC11B-02.note: Subject 'sonatas that the composer ... wrote for his pupils' takes main verb 'circulated' with no punctuation. The comma before 'wrote' (closing the appositive) baits A; C folds the verb into the relative clause; D dash mismatched. PHASE 2: Sound; explanation correctly rules out 'explains'/'agree' as main verbs.

SEC11B-03.note: Needs ', but' plus the subordinate 'because' clause so the comma after 1931 introduces the main clause. A/B produce splices; D makes 'the quarry flooded' a clause and the comma after 1931 a splice (strongest distractor). PHASE 2: Sound; D is a good comma-splice-at-a-distance distractor.

SEC11B-04.note: 'using ... vessel' opened with a comma after 'demonstrated', so it closes with a comma before the that-clause object. The internal dash pair baits A (dash would mismatch); B leaves the phrase unclosed and reads 'vessel that' as relative; C semicolon wrong. PHASE 2: Sound; dash-pair bait is well built.

SEC11B-05.note: Two independent clauses ('several species answer' is the second main clause after a fronted PP); semicolon. B splice, C fused (and misattaches the PP to 'return'), D however-splice. PHASE 2: Sound; fairly routine boundary item.

SEC11B-06.note: Comma closes the introductory Because-clause; 'Latin and Greek' is the main subject of 'were offered'. A is a garden-path trap (study Latin and Greek). C and D are strikeable on sight after a dependent clause, leaving a 50/50 between A and B. PHASE 2: Key correct. Minor imprecision: under A, 'languages ... were offered' could take 'languages' as subject; the real fault is the comma splitting that subject from its verb. Still supports the key. Two free strikes (C/D after a Because-clause) leave a 50/50.
